analysis.one_liner: Protects offshore oil and gas workers from being fired for reporting safety problems or refusing dangerous work.
analysis.headline: The House passed the offshore oil and gas worker whistleblower bill 315-93 in July 2010, but the Senate never voted and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for offshore oil and gas employers to fire or punish workers who report safety violations or unsafe conditions, report an illness or injury, testify in a proceeding, or refuse work they reasonably believe could injure people or cause an oil spill. A worker who was retaliated against could file a Labor Department complaint within 180 days, get an investigation, and win reinstatement, back pay, and damages. Employers would have to post notices of these rights, train workers on them within 30 days of hire and once a year, and hand out cards with a toll-free Labor Department complaint number.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas workers — rig and support crews, spill cleanup and emergency response workers, and job applicants — who would gain a federal right to report violations and unsafe conditions, refuse work they reasonably believe is dangerous or could cause a spill, and win reinstatement, back pay, and damages if fired for it. Coastal communities gain indirectly, because workers who feared a task could cause a spill could refuse it without losing their jobs.

how_it_helps.text: It would have barred offshore oil and gas employers from firing or punishing workers who report violations or unsafe conditions to the employer or to government officials, testify or help in proceedings, report an illness or injury, or refuse duties or exercise stop-work authority based on a good-faith belief that the work could injure people or cause an oil spill.

Workers would have had 180 days to file a Labor Department complaint, with an investigation and written findings due within 90 days, preliminary reinstatement that stays in effect while objections are pending, an administrative law judge hearing, and access to federal court if no final decision comes within 300 days.

Workers who won would get reinstatement with back pay and interest, compensatory and consequential damages, exemplary damages where appropriate, and attorney and expert witness fees paid by the employer.

Employers would have to post a notice of these rights at the worksite, train workers on them within 30 days of hire and once a year after that, and hand each worker a card with a toll-free Labor Department number for information or complaints.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators, contractors, and subcontractors: posting, training, and card costs, plus reinstatement orders, back pay with interest, compensatory and exemplary damages, and attorney fees when found to have retaliated against a worker.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers would face new compliance duties: posting a Labor Department-approved notice, training workers within 30 days of hire and annually, and distributing a complaint card — costs falling on operators, contractors, and subcontractors alike.

Preliminary reinstatement orders take effect before an employer's objections are resolved, because filing objections does not stay reinstatement — a speed-over-process trade-off an employer could fairly object to.

Retaliation cases would be hard for workers to win: they must file within 180 days and show the protected act was a contributing factor, while employers escape liability by clear and convincing evidence that they would have taken the same action anyway.
The deterrent against frivolous complaints is thin — an employer who prevails on a bad-faith finding can recover at most $1,000 in attorney fees from the complainant.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance side is cheap: a poster, annual training, and a wallet card. The real cost is liability for retaliation, which is the point — it raises the price of firing workers for reporting hazards. The design trades some employer process for worker speed, since preliminary reinstatement takes effect before objections are heard, but the bill builds in a hearing before an administrative law judge, an appeal to the Secretary, and court review, and it lets employers escape liability by proving they would have made the same decision anyway. The honest limits are scope (offshore oil and gas work only) and dependence on the Labor Department to actually investigate and enforce.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 315-93, attached its text to a bigger offshore drilling bill, and tabled the standalone version; the Senate never voted on either before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) introduced the bill on July 26, 2010, joined by Rep. Edward Markey (D-MA), and it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the same day.

Four days later, the House Rules Committee reported a rule bringing the bill to the floor with one hour of debate and closed to amendments except one pre-approved change; the House adopted the rule and debated the bill that same day.
The action history shows referral to committee on July 26 and a floor rule on July 30, with no committee markup or vote in between.

Rep. John Kline (R-MN) moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to insert a different whistleblower section; the motion failed 171-234, with 10 of 253 Democrats and 161 of 178 Republicans in favor.
The House passed the bill 315-93: 247 of 253 Democrats and 68 of 178 Republicans voted yes.
Under the rule, the bill's passed text was appended as new matter to H.R. 3534, a separate offshore drilling bill, and the standalone H.R. 5851 was laid on the table.
No Senate action followed; the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, and the bill died without a Senate vote.

The bill would have made it illegal for offshore oil and gas employers to retaliate against workers who report violations or unsafe conditions under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, report illnesses or injuries, testify, or refuse work they reasonably believe could injure people or cause an oil spill.

Workers would have had 180 days to file a Labor Department complaint, with findings due within 90 days, preliminary reinstatement that stays in effect while objections are pending, and court access if no final decision came within 300 days.
Employers would have had to post notices of these rights, train workers within 30 days of hire and yearly after that, and give workers a card with a toll-free Labor Department complaint line.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators, contractors, and subcontractors avoided the new posting, training, and retaliation-liability rules entirely; offshore workers kept whatever protections they had before.

for.name: George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 26, 2010 and had it on the House floor under a rule four days later.

for.name: Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction as an original cosponsor.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.role: Committee that decides which bills reach the House floor and on what terms
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule (H. Res. 1574) that brought the bill to the floor with one hour of debate and closed it to amendments except one pre-approved change.

against.name: John Kline
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to insert a different whistleblower section; the motion failed 171-234.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill, or the House-passed offshore drilling bill carrying its text, to a Senate vote; no Senate action was recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was broad but lopsided: 247 of 253 Democrats and 68 of 178 Republicans voted yes, and 92 of the 93 no votes came from Republicans; the failed motion to recommit split 161 of 178 Republicans in favor against 10 of 253 Democrats.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas producers and operators
industries.note: The bill would have made retaliation against workers who report safety violations, injuries, or spill risks illegal, exposing operators to reinstatement orders, back pay, and exemplary damages. Their interest in avoiding that liability runs against workers' ability to report hazards.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling contractors and oilfield service companies
industries.note: The bill's definition of employer explicitly covers agents, contractors, subcontractors, and consultants, so drilling and service contractors would bear the same posting, training, and liability rules as operators.

industries.industry: Oil spill cleanup and emergency response firms
industries.note: The bill covers workers in spill cleanup, emergency response, environmental surveillance, and restoration on the Outer Continental Shelf, so those firms would face the same compliance duties and retaliation liability.
